units.title: 1. Stroke and TIA Definitions
units.guide:
The chapter opens with the time-based definitions: stroke is abrupt focal/global neurological deficit lasting 24 hours or more with evidence of infarction or hemorrhage, while TIA is focal brain/retinal ischaemia lasting under 1 hour without infarction.
Diffusion-weighted MRI then separates the two: a normal DWI study means only TIA, whereas a hyperintense lesion means minor stroke even when the patient has clinically recovered.
The chapter's printed stroke line reads 'lasting ≥24 hrs' (OCR 'a4' = 24).

units.title: 2. ABCD2 Score Components and Points
units.guide:
The ABCD² score predicts the risk of stroke following TIA, summing points across five components: age above 60 years and BP ≥140/90 mmHg at initial evaluation give 1 point each; clinical features give 1 for speech disturbance without weakness and 2 for unilateral weakness; duration gives 1 for 10-59 minutes and 2 for 60 minutes or more; diabetes gives 1 point.
The points column digits were re-read glyph by glyph from the scan (each cell is a single digit).
Total score therefore runs from 0 to 7.

units.title: 3. ABCD2 Risk Stratification
units.guide:
The risk table stratifies stroke risk after TIA by total score at 2, 7 and 90 days: Low 0-3 = 1.0/1.2/3.1%, Moderate 4-5 = 4.1/5.9/9.8% and High 6-7 = 8.1/11.7/17.8%.
The High-row values were resolved glyph by glyph at high zoom (OCR had merged the digits) and match the Johnston Lancet 2007 validation table the book reproduces.
Risk rises monotonically with the score band.

units.title: 4. Antiplatelet Notes
units.guide:
The printed Notes state the key indications for dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) in neurology: TIA, mini stroke and intracranial atherosclerotic disease (ICAD) with more than 50% occlusion.
Every other condition gets a single antiplatelet.
For the DAPT combination the book ranks aspirin/ticagrelor above clopidogrel.

units.title: 5. Atherosclerotic Causes and Cerebral Venous Thrombosis
units.guide:
The causes section opens with '1. Atherosclerotic', which branches into arterial and venous disease; the venous branch is cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT).
CVT causes are split into inherited (Factor V Leiden mutation) and acquired (antiphospholipid syndrome, pregnancy/postpartum), with symptoms of raised intracranial pressure: headache, vomiting and seizures.
Arterial disease splits into ischaemic (85%) and haemorrhagic (15%).

units.title: 6. Ischaemic Subtypes and Embolic Sources
units.guide:
Arterial stroke divides into ischaemic (85%) and haemorrhagic (15%); the haemorrhagic examples are SAH, EDH and IVH, all managed by a neurosurgeon.
The ischaemic arm divides into thrombotic (large vessel, evolving, weakness rising over 48-72 hours), embolic (hyperacute, cortical features, rapid recovery, distal vessel) and lacunar (30-300 μm vessels, lipohyalinosis).
Emolic disease splits into cardioembolic (mitral stenosis, AF, prosthetic valve, dilated cardiomyopathy, recent MI within 4-10 weeks, sick sinus syndrome) and artery-artery (the m/c stroke, from neck vessels).

units.title: 7. Thrombotic versus Embolic Table and CT Imaging
units.guide:
The comparison table separates the two by tempo: onset (stroke in evolution versus hyperacute), features (↑headache versus LOC/seizures), weakness (rising over 48-72 hours versus full at onset), clot (fibrin clot versus red clot) and transformation (haemorrhagic transformation belongs to the embolic column).
CT imaging then shows the ischaemic stroke as a hypodense lesion and acute blood as a hyperdense lesion, with the three printed images being ischaemic stroke, haemorrhagic stroke and subarachnoid haemorrhage.

units.title: 8. Non-Atherosclerotic Causes and the Ischaemic Cascade
units.guide:
Non-atherosclerotic causes comprise moya-moya disease (multiple collaterals with 'puff of smoke' appearance from internal carotid artery vasculopathy), vasculitis, Fabry's disease, fibromuscular dysplasia, carotid artery dissection, dissection and Takayasu arteritis.
The pathology flowchart runs ATP depletion → failure of the Na+-K+ ATPase pump → glutamate release → calcium entry → liquefactive necrosis, on a Day 1 to Day 24 timeline captioned 'Hemorrhagic transformation of stroke'.

units.title: 9. Treatment Goals and Early CT Signs
units.sec: Treatment Goals and Early CT Signs
units.guide:
Goals of stroke treatment are revascularization (reperfusion), avoiding secondary injury and establishing collateral blood flow; the secondary-injury column lists 4-5 days of raised ICT (cerebral edema), SIADH/metabolic issues and haemorrhagic transformation.
Investigations rank MRI above CT, and the early CT findings in stroke are the hyperdense MCA sign (6 hrs) with the MCA dot sign as the earliest, the insular ribbon sign (6-48 hrs) and obscuration of the lentiform nucleus (8-24 hrs).

units.title: 10. Lacunar Stroke and Small Vessel Disease Markers
units.guide:
Lacunar stroke occurs in the elderly with F > M and hypertension as the risk factor; the handwritten definition note reads '…cm size infarct in a 30-300 μm vessel d/t lipohyalinosis'.
The types table maps pure motor stroke to the lenticulostriate artery and internal capsule, pure sensory stroke to the thalamogeniculate artery and VPL nucleus, and ataxic hemiparesis/dysarthria-clumsy-hand to the basilar artery and basi pons.
The MRI small-vessel-disease markers with their modalities are recent small subcortical infarct (DWI), white matter hyperintensity (FLAIR), lacune (FLAIR), perivascular space and cerebral microbleeds (T2'/SWI); microbleeds point to cerebral amyloid angiopathy and CADASIL is expanded in full.

units.title: 11. Ataxic Hemiparesis Pathways
units.guide:
Ataxic hemiparesis is the same as dysarthria with clumsy hands.
The pathway diagram shows corticopontocerebellar (CPC) fibres running cortex → basi pons → contralateral cerebellum and the corticospinal (CS) tract running cortex → pyramid → contralateral body; CPC damage gives contralateral cerebellar findings and CS damage contralateral weakness.
A lesion at the basis pontis therefore produces ataxic hemiparesis / dysarthria with clumsy hands, and the DRTC (Dentato Rubro Thalamo Cortical) fibres pass via the red nucleus while spinocerebellar fibres degenerate in Friedreich's ataxia.
